requirement_text: Non-Swiss upper-secondary school-leaving certificates are evaluated against the Swiss Maturität by requiring general-education content covering six subjects studied continuously over the final three years: (1) first/native language, (2) second language, (3) mathematics, (4) a natural science (biology, chemistry or physics), (5) a humanities/social science (history, geography, or economics/law), and (6) an elective from specified categories (e.g. informatics, philosophy, or a repeat of categories 2/4/5). This is the base recognition framework that each Swiss university's own admission regulations then apply, typically adding institution-specific numeric thresholds or additional conditions on top of it.
source_authority_note: swissuniversities.ch is the official site of swissuniversities, the national umbrella/coordinating body (Rectors' Conference of the Swiss Universities) for Swiss higher education; not a .edu/.ac./.gov domain but the closest equivalent to a national admissions-coordination authority in this system.
limitations: Page states this list is 'revised annually' and references 'academic year 2026/27', but does not state a single unambiguous entry year in a form we are willing to convert without inference, so cycle_year is left null rather than guessed. This six-subject framework was independently corroborated (near-verbatim) on UZH's, UNIGE's, and UNIL's own admission pages — see per-institution files — which is why confidence is 'high' despite extracted_summary fidelity.
researcher_notes: This is the base national-coordination layer. Cross-checked against UZH, UNIGE and UNIL's own restatements per coordinator instruction: all three describe the same six-category structure with no factual contradiction found on this specific point.

requirement_text: Recognition of a foreign school-leaving certificate for Swiss university admission is NOT a single centralized decision made by swissuniversities. swissuniversities' Chamber of Universities adopts and publishes coordinating 'Recommendations for evaluating non-Swiss secondary school leaving certificates' and an annually-revised country-by-country requirements list, but the swissuniversities.ch admission-requirements page itself states each university 'autonomously handles the question of academic recognition of both Swiss and foreign School Leaving Certificates and Academic Diplomas' and that 'the relevant legal provisions of each university are decisive.' The Swiss ENIC (national recognition information centre) FAQ similarly states Swiss ENIC 'is not responsible for evaluating school leaving certificates' and that institutions 'decide independently on admission to study programmes.' In practice this is a hybrid: a national coordinating framework (six-subject content standard, Lisbon Convention treatment, ECUS mechanism) that each of the 5 institutions then implements through its own binding admission regulations, which add their own specific numeric thresholds (see per-institution files for e.g. UNIGE's country-specific grade-average tables).
source_authority_note: swissuniversities.ch / Swiss ENIC is the national recognition information centre, hosted by swissuniversities; not a .edu/.ac./.gov domain.
limitations: This record deliberately captures the governance structure as a hybrid (national coordination + per-university binding decision), rather than flattening to either 'fully centralized' or 'fully independent per university' — both framings appear in the sources depending on which page you read, and neither alone is accurate.
researcher_notes: Directly addresses the coordinator's request to characterize governance carefully. No CONFLICTING_EVIDENCE found between swissuniversities' central pages and the Swiss ENIC FAQ — both describe the same hybrid structure consistently. See per-institution files for the cross-check against UZH/UNIGE/UNIL's own pages, which also did not surface a factual conflict on this point.

requirement_text: Certificates from countries that are signatories to the Lisbon Recognition Convention ('Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications concerning Higher Education in the European Region', ETS No. 165/1997) generally face reduced requirements compared to non-signatory countries: the secondary certificate plus a home-country university admission certificate is typically sufficient for most Swiss universities, without the ECUS complementary-examination requirement that applies to most non-signatory-country certificates. EU/EFTA country diplomas are generally recognized without the additional ECUS step.
limitations: General pattern only; exact treatment still varies by specific country and by institution (e.g. UNIGE's own conditions document imposes country-specific numeric grade-average thresholds even for Lisbon Convention / EU countries such as Germany and France — see UNIGE file). Not an unconditional exemption from all institution-specific requirements.
researcher_notes: Confirmed consistent with (not contradicted by) UNIGE's own conditions page, which references 'la Convention de Lisbonne' for its country treatment (per WebFetch of unige.ch/immatriculations/conditions).

requirement_text: For applicants holding a foreign secondary school-leaving certificate that is recognized as existing/valid but NOT deemed equivalent to a Swiss Matura by the university concerned, admission typically requires passing the ECUS (Examen Complémentaire des Hautes Écoles Suisses / Complementary Examination of the Swiss Universities) — a nationally centralized supplementary examination, not a numeric grade threshold. This is a categorically different requirement shape from a 'you need X score' rule: it is a pass/fail supplementary exam sat once per year in August, administered centrally, that stands in place of (or alongside) other admission criteria for applicants from many non-Lisbon-Convention or otherwise-insufficient certificate backgrounds.
limitations: Which specific certificates/countries trigger the ECUS requirement (vs. direct recognition) varies by institution — see per-institution files for UZH, UNIGE and UNIL's own country-specific ECUS triggers.
researcher_notes: IMPORTANT SHAPE FLAG: ECUS is a pass/fail supplementary examination requirement, not a scalar score threshold. Recorded as requirement_category_db='entrance_exam' per task instructions, and deliberately not translated into any fabricated numeric 'minimum score' — none exists for the underlying certificate; the underlying certificate's gap is closed by passing the exam, not by hitting a number.

requirement_text: The ECUS exam covers four mandatory subjects — French (written and oral), mathematics (written and oral), English (written and oral), and history including an introduction to law (oral) — plus one additional subject chosen for an oral exam from: biology, chemistry, physics, or geography (including introduction to economics). Exams are held at KME in Zurich (German language of instruction) and at GypAd in Crissier, canton Vaud (French language of instruction).
limitations: No Italian-language ECUS sitting location was found in the sources reviewed; not confirmed either way whether one exists.
researcher_notes: Cross-checked against UNIL's own page describing its ECUS pathway (which independently listed the identical four mandatory subjects — French C1, Mathematics, English, History+law — plus the same elective list and named Crissier VD as the sitting location). No conflict found between the central swissuniversities description and UNIL's own restatement.

requirement_text: The EMS (Eignungstest für das Medizinstudium / test d'aptitudes pour les études de médecine) is a centrally-administered, nationally-standardized aptitude test — 'the EMS is not a knowledge test.' It consists of eight task groups in multiple-choice format plus a subtest on 'concentrated and careful work,' testing thinking/memory ability and logical/spatial understanding rather than subject knowledge. The test lasts approximately four hours, beginning between 9:45–10:00 a.m. and typically finishing between 2:00–2:30 p.m.
source_authority_note: swissuniversities.ch official FAQ page, national coordinating body for medical-school admission; not .edu/.ac./.gov.
limitations: Some third-party test-prep sites (not official sources — e.g. medgurus.de) describe the EMS as '11 subject areas, 158 tasks, 255 minutes' with 'best 35% admitted.' We could not verify these specific figures against any official swissuniversities page and are deliberately NOT recording them; the official FAQ page we did fetch describes 8 task groups + 1 subtest over ~4 hours (240 minutes) and states no admission percentage. This is a case of an unverified third-party claim appearing to conflict with an official source — per the rules governing this research, only the official-source figures are recorded, and the unverified figures are noted here rather than silently discarded.
researcher_notes: Deliberately excluded the unverified '11 areas / 158 tasks / 255 min / 35% admitted' claims sourced only from WebSearch snippets of third-party test-prep sites, per the standing rule that search snippets are discovery leads, not evidence.

requirement_text: Eligibility to sit the EMS and pursue Swiss medical studies is restricted by citizenship/residence, not open to all internationally-qualified applicants: 'Foreign applicants without Swiss citizenship or long-term Swiss residence cannot study medicine in Switzerland due to [the] limited study places. A student visa or residence permit for education purposes is insufficient.' Only Swiss/Liechtenstein citizens or those holding an equivalent long-term residence status are eligible to sit the EMS test itself.
limitations: The precise legal boundary of 'equivalent long-term residence status' (settlement permit categories, spouse-of-Swiss-citizen provisions, etc.) is defined per-institution — see ETH Zurich and UZH files for the specific eligibility category lists found on their own medicine-admission pages.
researcher_notes: CRITICAL FINDING for ORYN: a purely international applicant (no Swiss/Liechtenstein citizenship, no long-term CH residence) generally cannot gain admission to a Swiss Bachelor in Human Medicine at the EMS-using institutions, regardless of academic strength. This should not be silently dropped when this university/program pairing is surfaced to international students.

requirement_text: Medicine is not taught in English anywhere in Switzerland: 'Teaching languages in medical studies in Switzerland are German and French. There is no medical program taught in English.'

The EMS is required for entry to Human Medicine at: University of Basel, University of Bern, University of Fribourg (German-language track), University of Zurich (UZH) including its Zurich-Lucerne and Zurich-St. Gallen partner tracks, Università della Svizzera italiana (USI Lugano), and ETH Zurich. EMS sittings are offered in German (Basel, Bern, Chur, Lucerne, St. Gallen, Zürich), French (Fribourg only), and Italian (Lugano only). Of the 5 institutions in this research set, ETH Zurich and UZH require the EMS; Université de Genève (UNIGE) and Université de Lausanne (UNIL) do NOT use the EMS or any numerus-clausus at first-year entry — see their own files for their distinct admission model. EPFL does not offer a Bachelor in Human Medicine at all.
limitations: ETH Zurich's own admission page independently confirmed EMS use ('a central test... at ETH Zurich, Zurich, Bern, Fribourg, and Basel universities') without separately naming the Lucerne/St. Gallen partner tracks or USI Lugano, but this is consistent with (not contradictory to) the fuller swissuniversities list, since those tracks are UZH/USI-affiliated rather than independent EMS-requiring universities.
researcher_notes: This is the central 'do not flatten institution-level variation' finding for medicine: Switzerland does NOT have one uniform medicine-admission pathway. EMS-gated (ETH, UZH) and open-first-year-plus-later-concours (UNIGE, UNIL) are genuinely different admission shapes, both coexisting within the same 5-institution research set.

requirement_text: Université de Genève (UNIGE) and Université de Lausanne (UNIL) — together with Université de Neuchâtel — do not apply a numerus clausus or the EMS test for admission to the first year of the Bachelor in Human Medicine. Instead they admit qualifying applicants to first year without a pre-entry aptitude test, and instead select for progression from 1st to 2nd year via a competitive 'concours' based on first-year examination results and available 2nd-year capacity. UNIGE introduced its concours starting 2017-2018 (Rectorate decision under Article 17(5) of the Geneva university law); UNIL introduced its concours starting the 2022-2023 academic year (Vaud State Council decision), replacing an earlier propaedeutic-exam-with-threshold model. Both remain subject to their own foreign-qualification admission rules for entry to first year.
source_authority_note: unige.ch official faculty of medicine page; not .edu/.ac./.gov. Corroborated by UNIL's own official page for its own concours (unil.ch/fbm), cited separately in the UNIL file.
limitations: First-year entry to UNIGE/UNIL medicine is still not unconditional for foreign applicants — normal foreign-qualification recognition rules (and, for UNIL, a specific 'Cantonal Regulation of 9 December 2020') still gate entry. What is specifically NOT required is the EMS test or a numerus clausus at the point of first-year entry.
researcher_notes: See per-institution UNIGE and UNIL files for the detailed concours mechanics (pass thresholds, ranking, repeat-year rules) sourced from each university's own pages.

requirement_text: Within the swissuniversities country-recognition matrix, ETH Zurich and EPFL are treated as a distinct 'special tier': rather than the standard secondary-certificate + ECUS pathway used by most other Swiss universities, applicants without a directly-recognized certificate instead sit each institution's OWN entrance examination (or a reduced version of it, where partial equivalence plus home-country university admission evidence exists). ETH Zurich's exam and EPFL's CMS/entrance-exam pathway are institutionally parallel in role but are NOT the same exam: ETH's is conducted entirely in German; EPFL's CMS pathway is oriented around French-medium instruction (EPFL requires French B2 for its Bachelor's programmes generally).
limitations: This record summarizes how the central matrix characterizes ETH/EPFL as a group; the two institutions' own exam mechanics are recorded separately and in more detail in their respective files, since they differ substantially in structure (ETH: reduced/comprehensive, 4 or 8 subjects, German; EPFL: CMS preparatory year or direct scientific+general-knowledge exam sittings).
researcher_notes: Do not conflate 'ETH's entrance exam' and 'EPFL's CMS/entrance exam' as one shared national exam — they are separate, institution-run pathways that happen to occupy an analogous structural role in the national matrix.

requirement_text: Non-Swiss secondary school leaving certificates from countries that are NOT signatories to the Lisbon Recognition Convention are subject to additional requirements beyond the base six-subject framework, as defined in swissuniversities' country-by-country list. This list is described as being 'revised annually.'
limitations: We did not attempt to enumerate the full country-by-country matrix (dozens of countries) as it was out of scope for this 5-institution research pass; only the countries independently covered by UNIGE's and UNIL's own admission pages were recorded (Germany, France, Hong Kong for UNIGE; general framework for UNIL). A future research pass specifically targeting the full swissuniversities country matrix would be needed for country-by-country coverage beyond what appears in this file set.
researcher_notes: Flagging this gap explicitly rather than silently omitting it, per instructions to note what was deliberately left unresolved.
